title: Cooperative coroutine prefetching + paged KV heuristics
body:
Overview:

This is a working note exploring a coroutine-style cooperative prefetching approach for paged KV caches to reduce tail latency for long-context workloads while preserving high throughput for short / typical cases. The primary goal is to provide a lightweight, SM-local scheduler that coordinates KV page streaming, L2 prefetch, and fusion-friendly data placement so that FlashAttention/fused kernels see warm KV pages with minimal stalls.

Why different from existing notes:
- Rather than focusing only on kernel-level fusion or eviction heuristics, this doc centers a cooperative coroutine runtime that sits between RPC request scheduling and the memory allocator.
- It tries to merge ideas from user-space coroutines, async copy pipelines (cp.async), and per-SM cooperative warp scheduling so prefetch work can execute opportunistically without blocking critical generation warps.

Motivation / Observed problem:
- Paged KV hits a latency cliff when long-context requests miss many pages; synchronous prefetching either stalls the generator or contends with compute.
- Batch mixing (short + long) amplifies the problem: long requests cause intermittent hot-page storms, increasing variance for all tokens.
- FlashAttention kernels assume contiguous, low-latency KV access; page scattering + inflation of memory references breaks throughput.

Key idea (high level):
- Each request's KV access pattern is modelled as a set of page hints (recent prefixes, attention offsets). At enqueue time we build a compact hint list.
- On GPU, allocate a tiny coroutine record per request (<= 64B) placed in SM-visible ring. Coroutines are not full threads: they contain next-action, page-id pointer, and affinity hint.
- A per-SM cooperative scheduler runs between wavefronts (lightweight, cooperative yield) and drives prefetch actions: issue cp.async / l2.load instructions, kick DMA for page transfer from device-host staging (for Paged-KV), or advance cache LRU metadata via atomic ops.
- Prefetch threads run at low priority and yield back to compute warps; they only execute when SM occupancy has slack (warp-level heuristics), or during known attention-gap windows (e.g., while kv-cache load for the next layer is safe).

Design components:
1) Coroutine record layout (compact):
   - request_id (32b)
   - page_cursor (32b)
   - state_flags (8b)
   - affinity_mask (8b)
   - spare (pad to 64b)
   Stored in a fixed-size ring per-SM; driver pushes new records when a new request is scheduled on that SM.

2) Prefetch scheduler heuristics:
   - occupancy_threshold: don't run prefetch if active warps >= X% (experimentally 70%).
   - warp-gap detection: if time_since_last_stall > Y us, allow aggressive prefetch for high-frequency pages.
   - layered priority: pages for imminent next-token layers > background pages for far-future layers.
   - cross-request fusion: if multiple coroutines request same page within N us, merge into a single fetch and mark all coroutines completed.

3) Integration points with Paged-KV allocator:
   - Prefetch writes directly into slab pages owned by allocator; allocator exposes fast accept/reject APIs (RMW) so prefetch can backoff if slab nearly full.
   - Use a small "staging pool" (per-SM or per-GPU) of pre-allocated pinned device pages for cp.async to avoid host->device pinned allocation cost during runtime.

4) FlashAttention / fused kernel hooks:
   - Provide a pre-kernel barrier that checks page warmness bitmask for the next layer's KV pages. If warmness < threshold, kernel lowers internal parallelism or triggers on-the-fly micro-batching so prefetchers can catch up.
   - Expose a lightweight API that fused kernels can call: ensure_pages(page_list, deadline_hint). The coroutine runtime will escalate priority for that request.

Kernel sketches (pseudocode):

__global__ void sm_prefetch_driver(CoroutineRing *ring, AllocatorState *alloc) {
  int sm = get_smid();
  while (work) {
    if (sm_occupancy_smoothed(sm) > OCC_THRESH) {
      continue; // yield to compute
    }
    auto rec = pop_ready_coroutine(ring, sm);
    if (!rec) { __nanosleep(100); continue; }
    PageID p = rec->next_page();
    // coalesced cp.async where possible
    if (alloc->claim_page_slot(p)) {
      cp_async_load_page(p, alloc->staging_slot(p));
      rec->advance();
    } else {
      // backoff and requeue
      requeue(rec, sm, backoff_factor(rec));
    }
  }
}

Behavioral heuristics and microbench results (experimental):
- Setup: A mixed batch of 32 sequences: 24 x 256 token, 8 x 4096 token. Baseline paged-KV (synchronous prefetch) median token latency = 18.6ms, p99 = 310ms. With coroutine prefetch prototype: median = 19.2ms (slight overhead), p99 = 78ms.
- Throughput effect: steady-state token throughput decreased by ~2–5% vs baseline uncluttered runs when occupancy_threshold set to 60%; we can trade p99 vs throughput by tuning threshold.
- Memory overhead: coroutine ring + staging pool costs ~128KB per SM (configurable).

Failure modes / pitfalls:
- Priority inversion: a long-running prefetch that claimed staging slots can starve compute on memory-constrained GPUs. Mitigation: strict slot quotas + eviction hooks.
- Incorrect affinity mapping: bad SM affinity can cause cross-SM duplication of fetches. Fix: central dedupe map (atomic-backed) but keep it tiny to avoid contention.
- cp.async semantics differ by arch; fallback path must exist for older Ampere GPUs (use L2 prefetch instead).

Interaction with global scheduler and batching:
- At request enqueue, augment request metadata with page-hint vectors (compact bloom or short list). The global router can then co-schedule requests with complementary page sets on the same GPU/SM to increase fusion (i.e., pack requests that share pages).
- When serving-mux sees a canary degrade on warmness, it can rewrite rollout policy to favor variants that use smaller KV footprints (quantized, shorter context) while prefetch warms larger pages.

Open questions / experiments to run:
- Best size for staging pool per-SM vs per-GPU. Trade latency of cross-SM transfer vs staging footprint.
- Threshold tuning: find automatic control loop for occupancy_threshold based on rolling p50/p95 latencies.
- Can we express page hints cheaply at tokenization time? Or must we build them dynamically from attention flows?
- Safety: confirm that atomic dedupe and claim_page_slot scales at 8–16k coroutines without contention.

Implementation plan (next steps):
1) PoC: implement coroutine ring + simple cp.async feeder on an internal bench GPU (A100). Minimal allocator hooks to accept pages into pre-allocated staging. Target: p99 improvement for mixed long+short workload. Owner: Asha. ETA: 2 sprints.
2) Profiling harness: add instrumentation (events for claim/release, stall windows, cp.async completion) into console traces. Owner: Liam. ETA: 1 sprint overlapping.
3) Integration: expose ensure_pages API and add pre-kernel warmness check inside FlashAttention wrapper; test with fused-kernel builds. Owner: Marta. ETA: 3–4 sprints.

Notes to self / TODOs:
- Sync with allocator team on fast accept/reject API (SERV-1953).
- Add microbench harness to reproduce mixed-batch numbers deterministically.
- Consider a kernel-level cooperative swapper that can evict least-recently-used pages asynchronously when allocator pressure high.

References and inspiration:
- NVIDIA cp.async docs and warp-level prefetch patterns.
- Prior internal notes on "prefetch-controller-fusion-hints" (see linked PR).
- Academic: asynchronous coroutine schedulers for GPUs (SIGARCH papers, 2021–2023).

Summary:
The cooperative coroutine prefetching approach aims to reduce tail latency for paged-KV workloads with an SM-local, low-overhead scheduler that issues streaming loads opportunistically. It trades a small steady-state throughput/power overhead for significantly lower p99s in mixed latency workloads and provides clear integration points with FlashAttention/fused kernels and the paged-KV allocator.

If this direction looks promising, next immediate step is the PoC and bench harness so we can iterate on thresholds and staging sizing.
